title: C501A — Driver Door Module (DDM) connector
introduction:
I use this reference as the driver door module’s address book: the drawing locates a cavity, and the matching table row explains its circuit. Power, ground, switch signals, illumination and network messages share the connector, but they have different jobs. The LIN bus carries local communication messages; it is more like the door electronics’ conversation than a simple on/off power feed.

Start with the connector identity, then match a cavity label in the drawing to Cavity in the pin table. Read across that same row for Circuit Number, Color, Gauge, Function and Terminal Part Number. Circuit identity and cavity location belong together; wire color alone is an incomplete address.

This is a reference-reading guide. The physical viewing side, gauge convention and metadata codes are not defined here, so the drawing and catalog entries do not establish probing orientation, wire selection or replacement instructions. Access, electrical testing and repair require their applicable procedures.

edits.why: I use the side housing outline and the separated upper cavities as landmarks within this drawing. Match the printed cavity labels rather than assuming the positions form a uniform grid. Gray-filled positions correspond to unassigned rows in the table; outlined positions correspond to assigned rows. That shading describes the documented layout, not whether a circuit works.

Cavity connects the drawing to the table; Circuit Number identifies the electrical path, while Function explains its role. Keep the network high and low descriptions distinct, and read switch-return and ground descriptions literally rather than treating them as interchangeable. Blank assignment fields alongside an unused entry describe the documented configuration, not a missing-wire diagnosis. After identifying the row, use its circuit identity in the applicable wiring or diagnostic procedure.

The Service Part and Engineering Shell columns provide different lookup identifiers, while individual pin rows have their own Terminal Part Number entries. I keep those roles separate so a shell identifier does not become an accidental terminal order. Material and Gauge remain catalog information; this table does not teach splicing, terminal removal or pigtail installation.
